# Electric light (arc lamp and incandescent lamp) (`electric_light`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by dynamo_electric_motor, air_pump_vacuum, glassmaking, ohms_law_circuits, practical_batteries, alternating_current_grid
- Core idea: Two carbon rods touched and drawn a few millimetres apart carry a dazzling arc; this needs about 50 volts and a mechanism that feeds the rods as they burn, and suits streets and halls. For rooms, a thin filament is heated white-hot by the current inside a glass bulb from which the air has been pumped out very thoroughly, otherwise it burns through in seconds. Carbonised cotton thread or bamboo fibre lasts hundreds of hours; drawn tungsten wire in a bulb filled with a little inert gas is far better. The filament must be thin and of high resistance so that many lamps can be fed in parallel at about 100 volts through thin copper mains, each with its own switch and a fuse.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking the lamp is the invention; it is useless without dynamos, mains, fuses, switches and meters, and Edison's achievement was the whole system
  - A poor vacuum: an ordinary piston air pump is not enough, it needs a mercury pump (Sprengel, 1865) and heating of the bulb while pumping
  - A thick low-resistance filament, which needs huge currents and impossibly thick copper mains
  - Crediting Edison alone: Swan in England showed a working carbon lamp at the same time and many earlier lamps failed only for lack of vacuum
- History: europe: 1802–1809 – Davy (London) and Petrov (St Petersburg) show the arc between carbon points; 1876 Yablochkov's arc candle lights Paris streets; 1878–1880 Swan's carbon filament lamp (Newcastle); 1904 tungsten filament (Just and Hanaman, Budapest); americas: 1879 – Edison's carbon filament lamp at Menlo Park; 1882 Pearl Street central station, New York; 1910 Coolidge's ductile tungsten; 1913 Langmuir's gas-filled lamp
- Read:
  - Robert Friedel & Paul Israel with Bernard S. Finn, Edison's Electric Light: Biography of an Invention (1986)
  - Brian Bowers, A History of Electric Light and Power (1982)
